#7679. The SEC has requested to delay climate rule arguments. What’s next?

Sustainable investing experts are not surprised by the delay and say it is expected to have minimal immediate impact.

Acting Securities and Exchange Commission Chair Mark Uyeda’s decision last week to ask the Eighth Circuit Court of Appeals to delay arguments for the agency’s climate risk disclosure rule did not come as a surprise to regulatory experts in the space.

While the change is expected to have minimal immediate impact, it sets the stage for a shift in focus for the SEC under the Trump administration.

The SEC issued its long-awaited climate-risk disclosure rule last March, nearly two years after it was first proposed — and amid over 24,000 public comments. Uyeda was one of two commissioners to vote against the rule’s approval. The rule was immediately met with multiple lawsuits that were later consolidated into the Eighth Circuit. The spate of legal challenges led the agency to stay the rule’s implementation in April.

Given the agency’s stay and the change in administration, Tom Willman, regulatory lead for artificial intelligence sustainability platform Clarity AI, said Uyeda’s decision came “as no great surprise.”

“It is nevertheless disappointing that investors will be deprived of much-needed financially material information related to climate related risks,” Willman said by email Wednesday.

Julie Gorte, senior vice president of sustainable investing at Impax Asset Management was more blunt in an interview: “The only person on the planet who didn't see this coming was Rip Van Winkle,” she said Wednesday.

Uyeda’s recommended pullback on defending the SEC climate rule follows his prior critiques of the rule. During the hearing on the final climate rule, in the weeks after it was finalized and in his Feb. 11 statement announcing the delay request, Uyeda maintained his belief that the SEC does not have the authority to promulgate the rule or require such disclosures.

Jenner & Block Partner Jennifer Lee, a former assistant director of the SEC Enforcement Division, said Uyeda’s position is “consistent with the new, Republican-led SEC’s shift back to focusing on ‘bread and butter’ investor disclosure issues.” Lee, who now represents companies and financial institutions in regulatory investigations and litigation, told ESG Dive in emailed comments Thursday that she expects that focus to include an emphasis on materiality, while looking to avoid “overly prescriptive disclosure requirements for public companies.”

The change in SEC posture, however, is expected to have a minimal impact for companies or investors, according to Willman and Gorte.

“The impact of this is going to be extraordinarily minimal, partly because it was never enforced in the first place,” Gorte said Wednesday. “So we never had better climate reporting stimulated by U.S. regulatory postures to begin with. And for U.S. companies, or for any company really, a lot of the big ones are probably still going to have to be reporting on all the same things that were in that rule because of [other jurisdictions].”

Willman echoed that note and said that many U.S. companies already voluntarily report climate risks due to investor demand, in addition to growing regulatory requirements both overseas in jurisdictions like the European Union, and stateside in California. New York recently reintroduced its own version of California’s climate disclosure laws.

Additionally, Stephen O’Day, a partner at Smith, Gambrell & Russell, noted the intervenors in the case could continue the rule’s defense, even though the SEC’s announcement indicates this iteration of the agency is not inclined to defend the rules. In the case of the climate rule, 18 states and the District of Columbia have signed on as intervenors to support the agency’s rule.

O’Day said a similar process happened after intervenors continued the defense for enforcement actions taken by the Clinton-era administration for violations of the Clean Air Act by coal-fired plants. Ultimately, the intervenors prevailed, and the Supreme Court upheld the actions.

“The proceedings pending in the Eighth Circuit involve challenges filed by multiple parties and intervenors, any of which could seek to continue defense of the SEC rules,” O’Day said. “So, while the court may grant the requested 45-day pause, it remains to be seen whether any such pause will result in the end of the SEC’s final rules.”

Regardless, sustainability programs and disclosures are expected to continue.

“Regulatory shifts don’t change the fundamental reality: physical climate risk is already priced into markets,” Lukky Ahmed, CEO of climate risk data and analytics platform Climate X, said by email Wednesday. Firms have a fiduciary responsibility to continue to assess, manage and disclose climate risks to their operations, Ahmed said.

“Integrating climate resilience and adaptation strategies isn’t just prudent — it’s essential for maintaining business performance, driving shareholder returns, and protecting communities," Ahmed said.

Despite the shifting federal policy stance, “there is a lot of faith that the drivers of sustainability remain in place no matter who is in anyone's White House,” Gorte told ESG Dive.

“If we don't solve the climate crisis, there are going to be … parts of the globe that are probably uninhabitable, or where people can't work outdoors in the summer. If we don't solve the biodiversity crisis, the prospects are even worse.” Gorte said. “So there are things that we have to do in order to preserve what we think of as life as we know it, and those drivers are going to remain in place.”

#7678. Don't Expect a Lame-Duck Supreme Court Vacancy (But There Are Other Nominations to Consider)

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

Both the NYT and Bloomberg reports that Justice Alito still intends to finish out the current Supreme Court term.

There has been rampant speculation that one of the older conservative justices (namely Justice Sam Alito or Justice Clarence Thomas) might choose to retire before the end of the year so that President Trump could name a replacement while there is still a Republican majority in the Senate. But that is all it is: Speculation.

I have previously predicted that neither Justice Alito nor Justice Thomas would retire during this presidential term (let alone this year). I adhere to this view.

Today, the New York Times and Bloomberg each report that Justice Alito has reaffirmed that he is not planning to retire this year, and that this week's election results have not altered his intentions.

Justice Samuel A. Alito Jr. has told people close to him that he does not intend to retire immediately from the Supreme Court, despite Democrats' commanding win in Senate contests on Tuesday, which means Republicans will hold the chamber for only a short time longer.

As a result, Republicans may have missed the window for President Trump to name a fourth or even a fifth justice to the Supreme Court in the final two years of his presidency.

Justice Alito shared his plans with friends after the election results were clear this week, according to two people close to the justice who spoke on the condition of anonymity.

The 76-year-old Alito, an anchor of the court's conservative wing, has been the subject of speculation that he might abruptly step down to let President Donald Trump fill the vacancy before Republicans relinquish control of the Senate in January. Such a move could extend Trump's imprint on the court by letting him add a younger, conservative jurist to serve for decades.

The chatter has continued even though Alito said in an interview with Bloomberg News in late September that he had decided to remain no matter how the election turned out. "I intend to stick around through this term," he said then, referring to the nine-month court session that runs through June. "I made that decision many months ago."

Alito indicated that stance hasn't changed despite the Democratic takeover in Tuesday's election, said the person, who asked not to be identified discussing a private conversation with the justice on Wednesday.

While there is no equivalent report on Justice Thomas, there is little reason to think he is going anywhere. Justice Thomas is on the verge of becoming the longest serving justice in the nation's history. Moreover, Justice Thomas has previously said he intends to spend at least 43 years on the Court. Were he to stick to that plan, he would have several more years to go.

While there may not be a Supreme Court nomination to keep the Senate busy during the lame-duck period, there are lower court nominations to consider, including nominees for the U.S. Courts of Appeals for the Fifth, Eighth, and Tenth Circuits. As Michael Fragoso notes in the Wall Street Journal, the lame duck may be Republicans' last opportunity to confirm conservative constitutionalist judges for some time.

Republican senators can make a difference and send a message by putting the Constitution first and confirming the originalist nominees now pending. Petty or parochial squabbles with Mr. Trump may get favorable headlines today but they will be forgotten in a week. A judicial appointment can last a lifetime.

#7675. "The Time, the Opportunity, and the Need to Reclaim the Republican Party from Trump and Trumpism"

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

I thought I'd pass along this smart and readable analysis from Bill Otis (Ringside at the Reckoning); as I've mentioned before, he and his coauthor Paul Mirengoff are my go-to people for hardheaded, pragmatic, but principled conservative views. They are probably on balance more conservative than I am, but I always much enjoy their legal and political commentary. An excerpt:

In an election where overwhelmingly the preeminent issue was affordability — in other and more candid words, the increasingly obvious decline in the standard of living huge numbers of people are feeling — what has Trump been occupying himself with? Here's a partial list: Building the White House ballroom (from which, in a tone deaf rendition that defies description) he gave his election post-mortem; re-doing the East Potomac Golf Course to make it a "premium" experience; building a Triumphal Arch no one asked for or thought about when they elected him; demanding prosecutions for imaginary vandalism at the Reflecting Pool; invading Greenland; making Canada the 51st state; re-naming Lake Ontario; re-naming the Gulf of Mexico; and perhaps most prominently, making sure his name gets put on the Kennedy Center even though he had nothing to do with its creation. Then there are numerous other items: Trump passports, Trump one-dollar gold coins, and "commemorative" $100 bills, to name three.

Exactly what does this Adventure in Narcissism seem like to the voter — actually, the millions of voters — who feel like they're being stretched thin? You don't need a florid imagination to answer that one. They gave their answer last night.

It's not like Trump has had no successes. He's made three excellent Supreme Court appointments. He has tackled corrosive and unjust racial preferences like no one else had the guts to. He declines to bow to transgender bullying. Objective economic data show that, whatever "feelings" may be, the economy grew at a healthy clip just this last quarter. He used force with Iran when, for nearly 50 years before him, Presidents were content to kick the can down the road as the mullahs got closer and closer to getting the atomic bomb.

These are considerable and important achievements, not less so because Trump often acts like an oaf. But his character flaws throw a wrench into nearly everything he does. It's less that he's an oaf than that he's a child, far too often content to do what's quick and easy while leaving to adults what's messy and hard. The catch is: He's supposed to be the adult. The main thing behind the failures that got Trump his butt-kicking last night is not his classlessness, his carefree attitude [toward] the truth or his gargantuan self-absorption.

The whole thing, as usual, is much worth reading.

#7672. DEI attacks are likely to refine and improve programs, experts say

The intense pressure to end diversity initiatives has led companies to scrutinize their policies. Many of the attacks will end up strengthening DEI programs.

The politicians, provocateurs and think tanks that in the past few years have worked to dismantle diversity, equity and inclusion may not appreciate the full consequences of their efforts.

They’ve used a variety of tactics, in the public and private sectors, including White House executive orders; lawsuits or the threat of lawsuits; shareholder proposals; and needling on social media. They’ve notched high-profile wins, most notably the Supreme Court’s ruling against affirmative action and capitulation at several companies, including retailers and brands that have ended or scaled back their DEI programs.

The successful challenges, inevitably, are forcing scrutiny of DEI practices. But they also provide an opportunity to reinforce DEI goals and execution, which David Glasgow, executive director of New York University’s Meltzer Center for Diversity, Inclusion, and Belonging, sees as a silver lining.

Indeed, the victories are hardly universal. Because diversity, equity and inclusion are good for business for a variety of reasons, most companies are not abandoning DEI. So far in 2025, Target, Nike and Costco are among those that have defended at least some aspects of their policies (in Costco’s case, vociferously). As the Heritage Foundation, a major DEI foe, noted in November, most Fortune 500 companies continue to publicly commit to DEI.

“It is a time for companies to refine and strengthen their inclusion efforts in ways that reduce the risk in the short term — because the risk is real, and we know that — and in ways that are sustainable in the long term,” said Adrienne Pulido, vice president of inclusion insights at Kantar. “So it is looking at both ends of the spectrum, in terms of being very clear about what inclusion means to their business.”

DEI is being pilloried as discriminatory and unfair, yet these systems are designed to create a business that is neither. That is, a business where employees have a variety of backgrounds and perspectives (diversity); hiring, promotion and other actions are executed fairly (equity); and the culture is comfortable and inviting to all who work there (inclusion).

“Unpacking what DEI is and what inclusion is, is part of this moment we're in and part of the conversation that companies need to have about their strategies,” Pulido said by video conference. “What does DEI mean to the business itself? What does it mean to the business and to the future business? Because the demographics of the country are changing, and our research shows that inclusion as a concept, as an idea, is very popular among Americans of all backgrounds.”

DEI goals for most companies are more important than ever because the markets for their products and services are more diverse than they were a decade or more ago, according to Effenus Henderson, who has worked in recruiting, staffing and succession planning at companies in the U.S. and abroad since the 1970s.

“This attack is amplified through the use of social media and technology and psychometrics, where emotions get aroused and reinforced,” he said by phone. “But fundamental to all this is that DEI is not about creating systems that are discriminatory, or about quotas, or a focus on one thing at the exclusion of others. I don't think organizations have really done that. What they have been doing is really trying to expand participation because of the growing demographic change that we're seeing.”

The need to develop DEI strategies that fit with and further business strategies dictates the involvement of leadership, according to Henderson. Too often, though, they are left to the human resources department, leaving companies at risk of adopting DEI programming that is ineffective and possibly indefensible.

“The companies that are able to navigate this generally are the ones where leadership has spent the time talking about it,” he said. “It's not just about reacting to the George Floyd situation or to civil rights laws or litigation. It's really, ‘How do we integrate this as a part of the DNA of who we are as an organization?’ If your organization is more performative, then they don't really understand how it helps to shape business strategy and policy.”

DEI should be treated like any other strategic priority, according to Tim Heneveld, country director for Pergolux in North America. With DEI under the spotlight, it’s a good moment to reassess whether hiring, workplace environment, leadership and operational strategies fit with broader aims.

“That means setting measurable goals, using data to track impact, and holding leadership accountable,” Heneveld said by email. “Some organizations are feeling pressure to scale back DEI, but I think doing so would be shortsighted. Instead, companies should refine their DEI strategies, aligning them with long-term business goals rather than reacting to what they are seeing in the media or any other outside factors. I've experienced, firsthand, workplaces can attract top talent, strengthen their teams, and improve retention.”

In some cases, companies are continuing with their DEI efforts, but changing the names of their initiatives or titles of their employees, experts said.

Crafting DEI initiatives and training is always a work in progress because businesses, markets and demographics evolve, according to Henderson. For many companies, that may mean avoiding those three letters of the alphabet, or the words “diversity, equity and inclusion.” But that, too, requires some thought, he said.

“Is continuing to refer to it under those banners still appropriate, and if I look at renaming it, am I doing that to help enhance our appeal to the markets of the customers and employees we serve? Are we doing it as a reactive, defensive thing for a short-term issue that's hot and heavy right now?” he said. “Get clarity around your objectives, the alignment with your strategies, and then decide whether how you are framing it today will work for you tomorrow and the day after. At some companies, it may mean one thing, and to others it may mean something else.”

The list of lawsuits against DEI programs tracked by the Meltzer Center is long, and getting longer.

Most of these claims invoke civil rights laws intended to end or prevent unfair hiring practices or contracts. Frequently that includes Title VII of the Civil Rights Act, barring discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex and national origin; Section 1981 of the federal code barring discrimination in contracts; and the U.S. Constitution’s equal protection clause, according to Glasgow. The Meltzer Center advises companies to avoid DEI practices that give preference to members of certain groups and involve a tangible benefit.

Evaluating whether a company’s DEI programs run afoul of the latest interpretations of these codes entails enlisting attorneys or other compliance experts.

“This has become a thriving legal practice area,” Glasgow said.

Any business strategy should always be grounded in risk mitigation, and this is just another place for companies to check, according to Henderson. Companies may learn that, to avoid risk, certain aspects of their DEI programs should change.

Others may find that they pass muster. In its proxy statement urging shareholders to vote against a proposal that could have weakened its DEI programs, Costco’s board of directors made clear that the retailer regularly evaluates its “practices concerning compliance with law, including evolving Supreme Court decisions.”

In describing how Costco obeys the law and does not discriminate in hiring, promotion and other practices, the board also provided a litany of protected statuses. This is a reminder that, while civil rights statutes are being leveraged to overturn DEI practices, they nevertheless do bar discrimination for a host of reasons. Moreover, any company that does business abroad will encounter antidiscrimination law that isn’t being disrupted by political activism the way it is in the U.S., Henderson said.

“If you look at Canada, Europe, Asia and South America, there are regulations and laws that support and value diversity,” he said. “So backing away from DEI may, in fact, create harm for your business strategies in other parts of the world. It's not a simple answer, and it just depends on who you are.”

While it may seem like DEI programs are quickly getting scrapped in order to avoid controversy, most are simply under review, Glasgow and others said.

“I think it's prompting a much deeper reflection within companies, not just on what is strictly legal or illegal in what we're doing, but on what has been working and what has not been working,” Glasgow said. “Could we be doing this work more effectively, in a way that actually helps us achieve our business goals, or helps us create the kind of culture that we want to create? Are there things that have been low impact, or maybe even have a negative impact, that we should get rid of, even if it's not for legal reasons? I think the moment that we're living in now could be a helpful reset moment for the field.”

#7668. Anna Rasche on the Hope diamond and the trope of cursed jewels in literature

Each year approximately six million people visit the Hall of Minerals in the Smithsonian Museum of Natural History to jostle for a glimpse of the infamous Hope Diamond. Many are afraid to get too close. This singular stone has passed through the hands of adventurers and royalty, heiresses and actresses. And according to legend it brought almost all of them to a bad end.

Today, the Hope epitomizes the “cursed gem.” An object as alluring as it is dangerous; all the wealth of a kingdom, condensed into something that could be forgotten in a coat pocket. But it is hardly alone. Evil jewelry lurks in our earliest mythologies, embeds itself in the pages of history books, and stands at the center of some of our most celebrated works of modern literature.

An early example is the cursed Necklace of Harmonia, wrought by a cuckolded Hephaestus, Greek god of the forge, as a passive-aggressive wedding gift for the daughter born of his wife’s infidelity. Nonnus describes the necklace as a golden tangle of snakes and eagles, encrusted with gems. The tragedies of Oedipus and that of Acteon, who was torn apart by his own hunting dogs, can be traced to this sinister family heirloom.

In India, the Sanskrit texts of the Bhagavata Purana tell of the Syamantaka, a jewel, perhaps a ruby, gifted by the god Surya to the mortal King Satrajit.

The Purana states: “It was the peculiar virtue of that gem, that if worn with all purity it would yield gold and prosperity of the kingdom but if worn by a man of bad character it would bring on his death.”

Indeed, as soon as the stone was in mortal hands it set off a chain of violent deaths. The impure men who possessed it were mauled by a lion, murdered in their sleep, and decapitated. Historians Anita Anand and William Dalrymple hypothesize that the legend of the Syamantaka is the original “curse” legend, one so often attached to important Indian gems.

In the seventeenth century the French gem merchant Jean-Baptiste Tavernier traveled to India, unbothered by any tales of curses. He returned to the court of Louis XIV with spectacular diamonds from the fabled mines of Golconda. One of them would eventually be recut into the Hope diamond. Though Tavernier wrote hundreds of pages about his travels, he never told how he acquired the blue diamond (good business for a gem merchant).

In the absence of a true account, a rumor took hold. It was said that Tavernier prised it from the eye of an idol, invoking a terrible curse. Word spread that he, like Acteon, was eaten by dogs.

What is known for certain is that this blue diamond was stolen during the French Revolution, smuggled into England, and recut to hide its royal French provenance. It reappeared decades later and significantly lighter, in the collection of banker Henry Phillip Hope. Today, most gemologists agree that the missing carats became dust on the cutter’s wheel.

But for a long time it was believed another stone was cut, a blue brilliant of about ten carats. It was said to be owned by the mad Duke of Brunswick, a voracious collector of gems who died exiled from his ancestral seat. The duke’s effects were sold at auction and the blue diamond disappeared. The Brunswick Blue is the mysterious stone, a maybe-sister of the Hope, that inspired the fictional gem called the Midnight in my novel, The Cursed Diamond.

The Hope reemerged in England in the1830s, amid a Gothic Revival where cursed jewels fit right into the zeitgeist. Anne of Geierstein by Sir Walter Scott, published 1829, tells of Lady Hermione, who turned to ash when her precious opal was touched by holy water. (It was Scott’s fiction that launched the still-enduring superstition of opals as unlucky stones). Murky origins aside, the Hope was displayed as a national treasure at London’s Great Exposition of 1851, alongside another Indian diamond with a sinister history.

The Koh-I-Noor, the “mountain of light,” was once a principal treasure of the Mughal Empire. It came into British possession in 1849 after a particularly heartless agent of the British East India Company extorted it from the last Maharaja of the Sikh Empire, the ten-year-old Duleep Singh. The ship that carried the stone to England was plagued by tempests and cholera.

When it was finally presented to Queen Victoria, she accepted it with reluctance, believing it cursed. Luckily for her, an addendum was soon added: the curse only applied to men. To this day the Koh-I-Noor remains in the Crown Jewels of the United Kingdom, a source of contention with India.

Inspired by the Koh-I-Noor, Wilkie Collins invented The Moonstone—the fictional yellow diamond at the center of his 1868 bestselling novel. In this ur-detective novel, a young Englishwoman lands in trouble after inheriting a gem stolen from a Hindu idol by her unsavory soldier uncle. The Moonstone’s success fixed the typical arc of a cursed jewel in the western imagination: illicit origins, greed-induced folly, and bitter ends for those who coveted what was never theirs.

In 1901 Lord Francis Hope sold his family’s blue diamond to cover debts he’d racked up partying his way around the globe with then-wife, American actress May Yohé (Yohé would die in impoverished obscurity, blaming the Hope Diamond for her troubles). For the next eight years the gem passed quietly between dealers and buyers, landing with famed jeweler Pierre Cartier.

Soon, newspapers were cataloguing the misfortunes of the Hope’s previous owners: kingdoms lost, carriages overturned, ships wrecked, heads removed. It is a dark and un-fact-checked history, allegedly encouraged by Cartier to add intrigue and close a sale with American gold heiress Evalyn Walsh McClean and her husband.

After the McCleans purchased the diamond, their lives were marred by tragedy: madness, addiction, political scandal, and accidental deaths. Even so, Evalyn wore the Hope until her death. “Bad luck objects, for me, are lucky,” she said.

The trope of the cursed jewel, a treasure that brings great joy and great sorrow, continues to captivate and inspire works of fiction. It lives in Tolkien’s One Ring. It goes on and on as the Heart of the Ocean in Titanic and burns bright as the Sea of Flames in All the Light We Cannot See. Now, in The Cursed Diamond, it manifests as an icy blue stone called the Midnight, my own humble addition to this enduring lore.

Anna Rasche is a historian and gemologist who has previously worked in the jewelry collection at the Metropolitan Museum of Art and as a curatorial fellow at the Cooper Hewitt, Smithsonian Design Museum. Rasche's debut is based on original research she conducted on the uses of gemstones in medieval medicine at the Cooper Hewitt Museum and on site in Italy. She lives in Brooklyn with her husband and infant daughter.

#7666. Judge advances McDonald’s McRib lawsuit that alleges deceptive marketing

A federal judge in Illinois on Friday did not dismiss a proposed class action lawsuit accusing McDonald’s McRib of misleading customers about the sandwich’s ingredients. (Photo from Getty Images)

A federal judge in Illinois on Friday did not dismiss a proposed class action lawsuit accusing McDonald’s McRib of misleading customers about the sandwich’s ingredients.

The plaintiffs allege that the McRib, which costs $7, is shaped to look like ribs and misleads customers in ads to think that it contains rib meat instead of cheaper pork cuts.

In Chicago, U.S. District Judge April Perry of the Northern District of Illinois dismissed some claims, but she did not accept the McDonald’s argument that a reasonable customer could expect the McRib to contain rib meat. Perry said ads of the rib-shaped patties could possibly be an attempt to defraud, but more proof was needed, according to coverage by Reuters.

“Plaintiffs’ proffered understanding of ‘McRib’ is not unreasonable or fanciful,” Perry wrote.

McDonald’s contends that it does not use hearts, tripe or stomach as McRib ingredients, which the suit alleges. The fast-food giant, which has sold the sandwich since 1981, said distinctive product names do not fool reasonable consumers.

“This lawsuit distorts the facts, and ⁠the claims are meritless,” McDonald’s said in a statement.

#7665. Judge halts CFPB firings

In the same order, the bureau was told not to delete any agency data or transfer its reserve funding to the Fed or anywhere else. The CFPB then reportedly placed most workers on administrative leave.

A federal judge has ordered the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau and its acting director, Russ Vought, not to terminate any agency employee except for cause related to job performance or conduct until March 3, when another hearing in the case will take place.

The bureau responded, however, by placing on administrative leave all employees except those asked to return to work by “the Acting Director, Chief Legal Officer, or another designee,” according to an email from the CFPB’s human capital operations manager that was seen by Bloomberg Law.

The court order on Friday came after the National Treasury Employees Union urged Judge Amy Berman Jackson on Thursday to block Vought from a “mass firing” it believed would affect 95% of the bureau’s workforce as early as Friday.

In the same Friday order, Berman Jackson demanded that the CFPB “not delete, destroy, remove, or impair” any data or agency records covered by the Federal Records Act.

Berman Jackson also ordered the CFPB and Vought not to transfer money from the bureau's reserve funds, other than "to satisfy” the agency’s “ordinary operating obligations.” That includes returning money from the CFPB’s reserve funds to the Federal Reserve, as Vought said this month he would do.

The data-related developments follow a declaration the CFPB’s former chief technologist, Erie Meyer, filed with the court Friday, warning that databases holding 12 years’ worth of information the agency has collected would soon be deleted and “irretrievably lost.”

Affected data would include “supervisory and examination records of financial institutions, enforcement action data, consumer complaints, personal consumer information, and market research records,” Meyer wrote.

Loss of data that tracks institutions’ financial behavior “would impair the Bureau's ability to identify risks and respond to emerging threats within the financial system,” Meyer wrote.

“This could destabilize markets, allow bad actors to exploit weaknesses in financial institutions, and undermine public trust in the financial system,” she wrote.

It would also open the financial system to market manipulation, Meyer asserted.

“Tech companies moving into financial services could gain an illegal competitive advantage by accessing sensitive consumer financial data or enforcement records, and the audit logs of that activity could be deleted,” she wrote. “This could result in unfair competition and undermine market integrity.”

That may serve as a reference to X Money, the payments tool set for launch this year in a partnership between card network Visa and social media platform X, owned by Trump adviser Elon Musk, who’s also seen as the architect behind the Department of Government Efficiency, which infiltrated the CFPB this month.

The deletion of CFPB data “would leave consumers without critical recourse in the event of financial harm caused by institutions under the Bureau's jurisdiction,” Meyer wrote. Further, she asserted, it would make the CFPB’s Consumer Response database “unavailable and/or unreliable, severely hamper — if not entirely take down — the Bureau’s website, and likely result in the loss of mandatory public reporting the Bureau has previously done.”

Friday’s order may represent a relief to CFPB employees, but it doesn’t apply to bureau employees who have already been terminated. The agency last Tuesday terminated roughly 70 probationary employees, then Thursday fired another 70 to 100 term employees – those whose contracts have set limits between one and four years.

Altogether, last week’s firings cut roughly 10% of the CFPB's workforce, according to American Banker.

The CFPB was not the only banking regulator to see workforce reductions last week. Roughly 500 employees at the Federal Deposit Insurance Corp., or about 8% of its workforce, accepted a deferred resignation offer from the Trump administration, Bloomberg Law reported Friday, citing a spokesperson for the agency.

The FDIC then terminated probationary employees, the outlet reported Monday, though the number of employees affected remained unclear.

An FDIC spokesperson on Friday did not detail how deeply certain units of the regulator were affected.

A lawyer representing the CFPB workers’ union laid out the urgency of Friday’s court action.

”I’m asking that they don't fire the entire agency tonight,” Deepak Gupta, a founding principal at Gupta Wessler, told the court, according to American Banker. “I don’t want to leave the courthouse without some assurance that the mass layoff is not going to happen and then become a fait accompli.”

The workers’ union asked Thursday for a temporary restraining order to stop the firings, but agreed to seek a preliminary injunction instead.

That mirrors a case in the U.S. District Court for the District of Maryland, in which the city of Baltimore sued the CFPB, claiming Vought’s move to return the agency’s funding to the Fed would effectively shut down the bureau “by fiat.”

The government agreed Thursday that Vought would refrain from transferring money out of the CFPB’s reserve fund or returning money to the Fed or Treasury until Feb. 28, or upon a “contrary order” from the court, Bloomberg Law reported.

Still, in the workers’ union case, Brad Rosenberg, a Justice Department special counsel, objected to the request for a preliminary injunction.

"We don't think any preliminary relief is appropriate at this stage because we don't think the plaintiffs are likely to succeed on the merits," he said, according to American Banker.

Among the employees the CFPB terminated Thursday is Julia Barnard, who served as the agency’s student loan ombudsman since last February. Her position is mandated by the 2010 Dodd-Frank Act.

“This work matters,” Barnard said in a statement issued by the Student Borrower Protection Center. “It’s a lifeline for borrowers and a safeguard against a system that too often fails them. Dismantling this function is unconscionable and will cost real people real money.”

Delaying any further moves to slash the CFPB workforce would at least give employees time to plan and budget for their personal futures. Employees of the agency are entitled by law to 60 days’ notice of job loss. But last week’s firings came with no notice and with immediate effect.

Further, terminations for cause (probationary employees, for example, were notified that they were deemed “not fit for continued employment because [their] ability, knowledge and skills do not fit the Agency’s current needs”) left those employees without access to severance, one lawyer with the CFPB told ABC News.

In Vought’s first week as the CFPB’s acting director, the bureau’s headquarters were closed to employees, who were ordered to stop all bureau work. A tip line was also set up for people to report on employees who might be conducting work.

#7664. American Woman Convicted of Receiving Military Training from ISIS in Syria

An official website of the United States government

Official websites use .gov A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.

Secure .gov websites use HTTPS A lock ( Lock Locked padlock ) or https:// means you’ve safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.

Today, a federal jury in Brooklyn convicted Halima Salman, 27, a U.S. citizen and former resident of Brooklyn, also known as “Umm Khattab al-Muhajir,” of receiving military-type training from the Islamic State of Iraq and al-Sham (ISIS), a designated foreign terrorist organization, in Syria. Salman was convicted after a two-week trial before U.S. District Judge Natasha C. Merle.

“The atrocities committed by ISIS, including mass executions, sexual slavery, and the systematic terrorizing of civilian populations, represent some of the gravest crimes of our time,” said Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg. “There is simply no excuse for aligning with or receiving military training from an organization responsible for such suffering. Today's verdict sends a clear message that those who support this death cult will be found and prosecuted.”

“With today’s verdict, Salman is held accountable for joining forces with a terrorist organization,” said U.S. Attorney Joseph Nocella Jr. for the Eastern District of New York. “ISIS ravaged Syria and caused havoc across the globe; our Office will continue to prosecute those who supported its murderous reign.”

“It’s been nearly a decade since Halima Salman sought military training from ISIS in Syria, and today justice has been served,” said Assistant Director Jarod Brown of the FBI’s Counterterrorism Division. “The FBI remains unwavering in its vigilance. We will continue to identify, disrupt, and bring to justice those who support foreign terrorist organizations and threaten the safety of our nation and our communities.”

As proven at trial, in September and October 2016, Salman’s parents traveled with her and her eight siblings out of the United States, ultimately destined for ISIS-controlled territory in Syria.

In late 2016 or early 2017, Salman was 18 years old and married to an ISIS fighter in Syria, where she voluntarily sought military-type training and received authorization to carry ammunition and an assault rifle from ISIS. Salman received a document certifying that she successfully completed that training, a copy of which was found on her husband’s cellphone after it was recovered from the battlefield. Also on her husband’s device were photos depicting Salman with an ISIS flag in the background and a video that shows her brandishing an AK-47 rifle.

The case was investigated by the FBI New York Field Office. The Justice Department’s Office of International Affairs provided significant assistance obtaining evidence overseas.

Assistant U.S. Attorneys Adam Amir and Amanda Shami for the Eastern District of New York are prosecuting the case, with valuable assistance from Assistant U.S. Attorney Andrew Reich, Paralegal Specialist Emily Woodruff and Trial Attorney Patrick Cashman of the National Security Division’s Counterterrorism Section.

#7663. James Patterson on dictators, historical fiction, and writing a world war II thriller

James Patterson may be one of the world’s most prolific and bestselling authors but there is no secret to his success. It comes down to curiosity and the asking of a simple question that has sustained writers since the beginning of time: What if?

For example: What if, before his rise to absolute power, Adolf Hitler killed his half-niece/mistress Geli Raubal in retaliation for her defiance? And what if he next used his influence over the police and press to have her death declared a suicide? And what if he then waged a campaign of terror against those individuals and institutions who wouldn’t fall in line with that story?

Such speculation served as the impetus for The Munich Affair (Little, Brown and Company; September 21, 2026), a historical thriller based on a true story co-written with frequent collaborator (and “a really wonderful guy”) David Ellis.

“I loved the whole idea. It’s been controversial for a long time,” Patterson says. “I like…taking a real story and then fictionalizing it….We don’t know for sure whether Hitler actually did kill [Geli Raubal].”

The debate is not a new one. Though largely swept under the rug in 1931, a few intrepid reporters—including German activist and journalist Fritz Gerlich—refused to kowtow to political pressure, risking grievous personal and professional reprisals in their search for truth.

“A lot of newspapers chased the story,” Patterson says. “One of them, Fritz Gerlich, wouldn’t give it up…and the reality is that Hitler put Gerlich into Dachau.”

In The Munich Affair, Gerlich—later shot dead at Dachau, the first and longest running Nazi concentration camp in 1934—teams up with (fictional) Detective Thomas Bauer and resistance figure Erich von der Haas in a series of covert operations designed to bring down Hitler’s regime.

Given today’s cultural climate, it’s a markedly timely and topical story for an author who prefers to keep his prose free of politics.

“I don’t talk much about politics,” Patterson says. “But we certainly have a world now, and probably for some time, where we have…dictatorial leaders in several countries.”

And while the authors’ intent wasn’t necessarily to inspire readers to make comparisons between current world leaders and Hitler, perhaps that outcome was inevitable.

“When you read it, you will,” Patterson says. “And I didn’t try to do this, per se…but you do feel some of the things and you go, Hmmm, it sounds like some of the things that are going on now.”

Patterson likens the atmosphere during Hitler’s rise to power and authoritarian rule—in which he was able to declare himself Führer (merging the roles of chancellor and president into one) by manipulating the democratic system and suspending civil liberties—to modern-day aggression, whether North Korea’s totalitarian dictatorship or national operations such as ICE, whose extreme tactics undermine a legitimate issue.

“So, I think [the book] is kind of timely,” he says. “We can think about it and wonder, if to some extent, people blame the Germans for not rising up somehow and overcoming the Nazis…and somehow allowing, or turning a blind eye to, what happened in Germany….”

Which begs the question of whether future generations might reflect on current days with similar retrospect.

“Maybe at some point people will look at this country and ask, ‘Why didn’t we stand up a little bit more and deal with some of the things that are going on now?'” the author says.

Regardless, Patterson maintains that his primary responsibility is to entertain; any education or enlightenment that results is a plus, not the priority.

“You lay out a story, you lay out some information, and you let [the readers] figure it out,” he says. “I’m not a fan of editorializing. I try not to do too much of that.”

Though a departure, the book’s historical context is not unprecedented in Patterson’s wide-ranging oeuvre (which has sold an estimated four hundred and twenty-five million copies worldwide).

It’s something he first experimented with in 2003’s The Jester (co-written with Andrew Gross), in which an innkeeper-turned-pilgrim becomes disillusioned during Europe’s First Crusade and deserts the cause only to devastating consequences.

Like The Jester, The Munich Affair opens with a modern-day prologue, though the book extends this framework to include a secondary storyline in which a contemporary scholar—Eleanor Robbins, a history professor at the University of Chicago—is drawn into the mysteries of the past and travels to Germany to secure evidence of Hitler’s final moments with Raubal.

“In terms of storytelling, it makes it interesting to have her in there, dealing with Neo-Nazis right now,” Patterson says. “You get a feel for a ‘real’ person in the present day…trying to come up with the truth and being in a little bit of danger.”

While her character infuses the narrative with urgency and resonance, Robbins (like Bauer) also underscores the fact that the book is fiction, albeit grounded in the realities of the historical record.

The author recognizes this blurring of the lines for what it is, in contrast to works “masquerading as nonfiction”—such as the hundreds of books written about Shakespeare despite the fact that very little of his life and literary career can be stated with absolute certainty.

For a more comparable example of his intent, Patterson points to Norman Mailer’s anti-Vietnam novel, The Armies of the Night (provocatively subtitled History as a Novel, the Novel as History), which is considered a seminal work in creative nonfiction—a hybrid genre that combines the substance of fact with the style of fiction.

“He would create a lot of scenes and they would be, in his opinion, accurate. But they were still scenes,” Patterson says. “Some people would say, ‘Well, that’s not fair. You can’t do that in non-fiction.’ But he felt you could.”

It’s a similar approach Patterson takes with his own fact-based works, whether fictionalized like The Munich Affair or non-fiction books about tragic figures such as the Kennedys, Marilyn Monroe, and John Lennon or his collaboration with Vicky Ward on a more contemporary crime story, The Idaho Four (and their forthcoming book on Luigi Mangione, American Rage).

“Okay, here’s a scene and obviously I can’t know all the dialogue, but I have a sense of what went on,” he says of his intent to capture the essence of truth. “I think it’s okay as long as you tell people what you’re doing and then they can make their own judgments about it.”

Of course, there are times when creative liberties prevail—particularly when considering the demands of a thriller; such is the case with The Munich Affair’s combustible conclusion.

“We took a lot of license with the ending, but I thought it was…poetic, philosophical. It was an interesting way to pull it all together,” Patterson says. “I think you feel the fiction taking over a bit, but that’s okay, because we’ve had a big dose of [history]….Ultimately, we’re going to get to the bunker.”

Hitler retreated to Berlin’s underground Führerbunker in January 1945, as Allied and Soviet forces began to overtake Nazi strongholds and infiltrate Germany, signaling an imminent end to war.

It’s here that Hitler and his new wife, Eva Braun, died by suicide on April 30. Both ingested cyanide, and Hitler also shot himself in the head with a pistol. Their bodies, once discovered, were then taken to the garden of the Reich Chancellery, where they were set ablaze with petrol for cremation.

Despite official confirmation of this scenario, speculation as to how they died—or even if they died—has persisted to this day. It’s the stuff that conspiracy theories and historical thrillers are made of.

“I don’t think a lot of people are going to guess the ending on this sucker,” James Patterson vows. “They think they know, but they don’t know.”

It’s a promise backed up by decades of writing and hundreds of books, all of which are meant to keep readers turning the pages while asking what next?

John B. #7661. The best crime novels, mysteries, and thrillers of the month: November 2026

ghbvfgbhvnNovember brings cold winds and chilling adventures, with many of the year’s most intriguing gothics and noirs packed into the month ahead. Most of the following are clear crime and mystery novels; there are two books on the list below that are first-contact thrillers, but I figured their strong X-Files vibes enough to make them count as mysterious.

Thanks to my colleagues Olivia Rutigliano and Dwyer Murphy for their contributions.

Donna Freitas, Wolves of Summer (Soho Crime)

Donna Freitas has already proven herself one of the most fearless and fascinating writers around, especially with the suspense story Her One Regret, which addressed a taboo subject—motherhood, regretted—with compassion, understanding, and nuance. Her newest work, which I devoured in a single day despite the near-500-page length, expands on her previous book’s universe, with a glimpse into character Diana’s first case, as neighbors in a Rhode Island seaside suburb search for a missing girl, and are forced to confront their own long-buried traumas, reemerging in the wake of the preteen’s disappearance. Freitas is particularly concerned with examining the male gaze, the public nature of girlhood, and the terrifying experience of incipient womanhood on the world’s stage. Wolves of Summer should be noted as a mystery of some complexity; craftsmanship shines throughout the novel, and the denouement is perfection. –MO

I haven’t read such a thorough condemnation of such a corrupt little town since Red Harvest. (Almost) everyone in this novel is culpable, although very few of them realize what they are even culpable of, even as the consequences of their actions spiral outwards to the public gaze, and even as the town becomes known nation-wide for both its heinous crimes and its callous attitudes. Harold Rogers sets his tale in Steubenville, Ohio, exploring the lead-up to and and aftermath of a horrific crime, to which the townspeople respond even more horrifically. Rogers’ linguistic prowess and creative talents are on full display here, but never in a way that detracts from understanding the story or its terrible underlying message. A literary tour-de-force, and a noir masterpiece. –MO

Brendan Flaherty, Middleman (Atlantic Crime)

A middle-aged everyman struggling with family life and mounting debts gets drawn into a wild grave-robbing scheme when he moves to a small town with shadowy secrets. Flaherty is a writer on the rise, and his charms are on full display in this new novel, with a story full of big characters with subtly powerful arcs. –DM

Keletso Mopai, We Belong to the Trees (Seven Stories Press)

In immediate post-Apartheid South Africa, a ranch hand is accused of murdering a white farmer, sparking terrible rumors and increasing divisions in their remote township. Mopai uses a kaleidoscopic set of narrators to fill in the gaps and carry the truth forward to a day that can stand to hear it. –MO

Alan Bradley, Numb Were the Beadsman’s Fingers (Bantam)

My heart broke upon hearing of the recent passing of Alan Bradley, the author of the brilliant Flavia de Luce mysteries—not only because I will greatly miss Flavia, but also because I had the chance to meet him personally and discovered him to be as lovely as I could have hoped. Numb Were the Beadsman’s Fingers is his final Flavia novel (his twelfth!), and if ever there were a book to go out on, it’d be this one. It’s about a dead nun, a decades-old case, and a mysterious false identity. RIP to Alan Bradley, and long live Flavia de Luce. –OR

Ian Rankin, The Heights (Grand Central/Cardinal)

Ian Rankin’s stylish, modern take on a very classic mystery premise is a fun addition to November’s literary roster. The story is set in London, in an opulent high rise apartment overlooking Hyde Park. The residents are both impossibly wealthy and glamorous. And when, one night, the nighttime concierge is found dead, they are all suspects. Wheeeee! (This book also has the distinction having a sleuth whose name made me, a silent film fan, do a double-take: Gillian Gish).–OR

This one takes place in the same world as Braking Day, Oyebanji’s mind-bending locked-space thriller of generation ships and factionalism, and functions well as a prequel. Line of Descent asks, what could motivate someone to go so far as to kill amidst the high stakes of disrupting order on a colony ship? Readers might end up surprised, but they will certainly feel satisfied. –MO

Saba Brelvi, The Squatters (The Dial Press)

A well-to-do Muslim woman volunteering at a refuge center strikes up an uneasy connection with two of the migrants interned there, a pregnant woman and her husband, and begins helping them find shelter. After putting them up in a friend’s empty cottage, the woman and her family become the focal point for xenophobic reactionaries in the neighborhood and beyond, even as their connections with their community and their close friends begin to fray irreparably. The Squatters asks essential questions for the present day, and finds no easy answers. What do we owe to our communities, our selves, and our principles? Can a life have meaning without risk? Can words have meaning without subsequent action? And why don’t more books have references to the diggers? Read this shattering work of fiction at your own peril, for you might find yourself, too, standing up for your long-suppressed beliefs no matter the consequences. –MO

Sacha Naspini, The Witch’s Mouth Translated by Clarissa Botsford  (Europa)

Grave robbing in Tuscany from ancient Etruscan graves has been big business since before the war, but with new regulations cracking down on antiquities smuggling elsewhere in Italy, the little band of thieves at the center of the novel face new gangs trying to muscle into their territory, renewed inquiries from weary local authorities, and internal divisions that threaten to dissolve their operation entirely. –MO

Kennedy Cole, There Used to Be People Here (Berkley)

When a queer man dies in a gay bar restroom under, shall we say, unusual circumstances (a giant worm emerges from his mouth and leaves behind the mere husk of a body), two detectives go looking for answers, only to stumble upon a government conspiracy to cover up an alien crash site with deadly cargo. Kennedy Cole uses the language of science fiction to explore the experience of queerness as a person of color; one of the detectives is the first Black policeman in his small southern town, and he’s as drawn to the alien as he is repelled by his colleagues. A moody, atmospheric take on the first encounter thriller, with plenty of body horror thrown in (or perhaps, bursting out). –MO

Molly Odintz is the managing editor for CrimeReads and the editor of Austin Noir, now available from Akashic Books. She grew up in Austin and worked as a bookseller before becoming a Very Professional Internet Person. She lives in central Texas with her cat, Fritz Lang.

#7660. Karin Slaughter on Mo Hayder, thrillers by women, and the legacy of “Gone”

I clearly remember the first time I read Mo Hayder. Birdman was published in 2000, a year before my own first novel was published, and I felt an intense sense of wonder with every finely crafted sentence. The plotting was fantastic. The characters were not just believable but brought out an array of emotions from lust to disappointment to love to abject fear. The tension knotted more tightly with every turn of the page. I had never read anything like it—and it made me feel more inspired, more challenged, in my own career.

At the time, the genre was a hard place for women. We are supposed to be sugar and spice, the docile victims of these sorts of stories, not the ones who gain control and agency by writing about them with an unblinking eye. That Mo was able to accomplish this, that she broke ground for the many who came behind her, will always be an enduring part of her legacy.

The women who were able to follow, from Gillian Flynn to Ivy Pochoda to Jennifer Hillier, owe a tremendous debt to Mo for helping carve out space in a genre that often celebrates women on the page, but seldom celebrates them the same way in life.

But that’s exactly who Mo Hayder was: a mold-breaker. She was an iconoclast who could not be put in a box, neither as a person nor as a writer. She was bold. Her wit razor sharp. Her humor quirky. She didn’t shy away from writing about very dark things, and that made her an outlier. Her voice on the page was always confident and assured but never bordered into authorial intrusions. She never wrote the same book or told stories the same way twice. Mo Hayder was an icon.

In Birdman, Jack Caffery is a young, driven, seemingly unshockable detective who is faced with the daunting task of hunting down a serial killer who’s leaving behind a trail of horrific crimes—but the story is much more than the plot. Caffery is a character who grabs you by your bones and shakes you into seeing all the darkness in the world. He has messy relationships. He screws up a lot.

But in the end, you’re rooting for him—not just because you want the crime solved but because you want something, anything, to finally go his way. Readers often take it for granted that they will care about a character, but making them care about a character who does unlikable things is the difference between a writer and a master storyteller. Mo certainly deserves that title.

Gone is the fifth book in the Jack Caffery series but it stands very well on its own. By this point, Caffery’s counterpoint, Police Diver & Sergeant Phoebe “Flea” Marley, has been introduced. Marley is a lot like Mo: determined, beautiful, incredibly capable, but not invincible.

Flea and Caffery should have a closer relationship. They would fit together like two puzzle pieces. Unfortunately, they both carry around an awful lot of baggage. While this is tough for them, it makes them come alive on the page. They are excellent counterparts as detectives, and by the end of this novel you’ll be rooting for them both, despite their very deep flaws.

It’s no surprise that Mo won the Edgar® Award for Gone. She takes what already worked so well in this series and pushes up the volume by a thousand. The villain is completely fresh and extremely frightening. The plot takes amazingly satisfying twists that you’ll never see coming. And the story will creep and crawl right under your skin where it will stay forever.

Mo Hayder’s novels are dark, visceral, bold, and brilliant, and she leaves behind a lasting legacy. When she passed away in 2021, the crime writing world was devastated—tributes poured in and readers found solace in her novels—the incredible, brave, important stories she left behind.

Mo was always a writer—and a person—who looked at life as a question to be answered, as shown by her varied career path—not one to simply sit down to write in a vacuum, she made sure she had a wealth of life experience under her belt (she worked as a barmaid, security guard, filmmaker, hostess in a Tokyo club, educational administrator, and a teacher of English as a foreign language, to name but a few). Mo also held an MA in film from The American University in Washington, DC, and an MA in Creative Writing from Bath Spa University.

Writing was her love and her craft, and she took it very seriously. The legacy she leaves behind is not only that of a thriller writer, but of a generous, smart, passionate author and champion of other authors. I remember her as someone who squeezed every ounce out of life and did us all the great kindness of pouring some of that energy into her novels.

Over her many years as a writer, Mo, whose real name is Clare Dunkel, and detective Jack Caffery earned a legion of loyal fans, with Mo’s compulsive stories becoming staples of every crime reader’s bookshelf up and down the country—and indeed, across the globe. The series went from strength to strength, and Mo’s unique writing style and her refusal to shy away from the darker side of life became more and more apparent, setting her apart from other thriller writers and making it impossible for anyone to replicate her.

I am to this day still in awe of her tremendous talent and am deeply saddened that she is gone. We are so lucky that her work lives on.

#7659. ‘Judge Stone’ by Viola Davis and James Patterson wins inaugural Scott Turow Prize for Legal Fiction

Viola Davis (left) and James Patterson appeared in New York City in March for a discussion of their book, “Judge Stone,” which was chosen as the winner of the inaugural Scott Turow Prize for Excellence in Legal Fiction. (Photo by Dia Dipasupil/Getty Images)

Judge Stone, by acclaimed actor Viola Davis and prolific author James Patterson, has been chosen as the winner of the inaugural Scott Turow Prize for Excellence in Legal Fiction.

The prize, which is being awarded by the ABA Journal, the University of Miami School of Law and the University of Miami College of Arts & Sciences, was determined by a panel of judges that featured former ABA Presidents Deborah Enix-Ross and Carolyn Lamm, California Court of Appeal Justice Lee Smalley Edmon and Turow himself.

A public poll hosted by the ABA Journal also chose Judge Stone as the favorite for the prize from among the field of three finalists, which also included A Pair of Aces by Marie Benedict and Victoria Christopher Murray, and Grave Danger by James Grippando.

The Turow Prize aims to honor the work that best illuminates the role of lawyers in society and their power to effect meaningful change. It is a successor to the prestigious Harper Lee Prize, which the Journal and the University of Alabama previously awarded to outstanding works of legal fiction, including novels by John Grisham, Michael Connelly and Grippando.

Judge Stone is a legal thriller about a Black woman judge from a small town in Alabama who presides over a controversial case. It is the first collaboration between Davis and Patterson.

Davis is one of a select group of celebrities who are “EGOT” winners for taking home Emmy, Grammy, Oscar and Tony awards. In 2025, she was honored by the Golden Globes with the Cecil B. DeMille Award for “outstanding contributions to the world of entertainment.”

She won an Emmy for TV’s How to Get Away with Murder and has appeared in numerous films, including Academy Award–nominated Doubt, The Help and Fences (for which she received the Oscar). She won two Tonys (for Fences and King Hedley II) and a Grammy for best audiobook, narration and storytelling recording for her memoir, Finding Me. She also took home a Screen Actors Guild Award for her role in Ma Rainey’s Black Bottom.

In his long career, Patterson has created notable characters and series including Alex Cross, the Women’s Murder Club, Jane Smith and Maximum Ride. He’s written true stories about the Kennedys, John Lennon and Tiger Woods, and has coauthored No. 1 bestselling novels with Bill Clinton, Dolly Parton and Michael Crichton. He’s received an Edgar Award, ten Emmy Awards, the Literarian Award from the National Book Foundation and the National Humanities Medal, according to jamespatterson.com.

Named in honor of pioneering attorney and international bestselling author Scott Turow—the “father of the modern legal thriller”—the Turow Prize seeks to unearth compelling works of fiction that illuminate the dynamics of law, the justice system and the human experience.

Turow’s 13 fiction and two nonfiction books, including Presumed Innocent and the current Presumed Guilty, have sold over 30 million copies worldwide and been adapted for film and television.

Davis and Patterson will receive a cash prize and a signed copy of Presumed Innocent at the award ceremony and reception on Nov. 19 hosted by the University of Miami, along with the exclusive right to feature the prestigious Turow Prize logo on their winning book’s cover.

#7657. How Alain Delon Got Caught Up in a Murder Investigation at the Height of His Fame

The actor lies still. Eyes closed. Waiting for the signal.

‘Silence sur le plateau . . .!’ shouts director Jacques Deray.

The crew falls quiet. A silence descends upon the Saint-Tropez villa. Just the clicking of the cicadas, drunk on the late-summer heat in the scrubland surrounding the azure pool. Thick cables everywhere. Lighting rigs. Flight cases.

‘. . . Moteur . . . Ça tourne . . .’ calls the assistant director.

The camera motors fire up, a soft clicking as the film turning on the reels gets up to speed. The entire crew poised, ready . . .

The camera pans slowly across the glimmering, phosphorescent surface of the swimming pool until, languidly, it finds him: bronzed, lean, 33. Reclined by the water. Dark hair resting on hot sandstone slabs. A glass of orange juice perched on his belly, rising and falling with his breath.

His other hand toys with the water’s surface. Delicately it is withdrawn. Glistening droplets run the length of his fingers and drip sensuously onto his face, revealing to the camera for the first time one of the most famous men in the world.

Not Narcissus, but something colder, l’homme fatal. Nonchalantly, from being mesmerized by the water’s surface and his own reflection, he turns his head towards the sky, raises the glass from his chest and pours the juice into his mouth, slow and sensual.

Dark glasses on. Eyes closed. Pinned to the tiles by the late-summer heat. The remnants of the orange juice drying on his tanned skin.

He is, for now, untouchable. At the height of his powers.

Once the initial observations are complete, the two forensic pathologists begin the next phase of the autopsy. They make a clean incision across the scalp and peel the skin down on either side, revealing the smashed cranium beneath. The top of the skull is sawn off, the brain removed. Next, they open the torso, slicing through the abdomen to extract the vital organs. No major anomalies, except the liver. Enlarged, discoloured. Consistent with long-term alcohol abuse.

Once the examination is complete, the organs, including the brain, are placed back in the body cavity. The skull is reassembled; the skin pulled back into place and stitched at the crown. Fingerprints are taken and sent to the central police archives in Paris. The man still has no name.

Based on decomposition, the doctors estimate the time of death to be a week earlier, most likely during the night of 22 to 23 September. In their report, they write plainly: the skull had ‘completely collapsed in’. Cause of death: blunt force trauma to the head with a heavy object. The theory holds – for now – that it was a fight, something that got out of hand.

They sign the paperwork. The report is dispatched to the investigating judge.

Patard reads the autopsy report and gives the photographs a cursory glance. He can’t place it, but something feels off.

It’s the hands that catch his eye. Everyone insists the victim is a vagabond. But how many vagabonds have manicured nails?

The next day, a fingerprint match comes through. The deceased is one Stevan Markovic. Thirty-one years old. Born in Belgrade, 1937. The same prints first appear on records in 1958, when this man applied for political asylum in Paris. Then again:

Prison in Chambéry, 1962 La Santé, Paris, 1965 Namur, Belgium, 1964 Annecy, 1967

His last registered address? 22 Avenue de Messine, in the prestigious 8th arrondissement on the Rive Droite. A stone’s throw and the quartier of the Elysée Palace.

Then another twist. When cross-referenced, it would appear that 22 Avenue de Messine is also home to a famous actor: Alain Delon.

A file arrives from the Brigade Mondaine – the Paris vice squad. Technically tasked with investigating moral crimes, the Mondaine is unofficially tasked with monitoring the rich.

Patard flicks through their dossier on Delon, it’s only a few pages long; a couple of minor run-ins with the law. But then there are the photos: Delon with known gangsters, Corsicans, men who once fought for the Resistance and now run rackets out of Pigalle or control the ports in Marseille.

Who exactly is this Delon? Patard wonders. He calls in two detectives. ‘Go to Avenue de Messine,’ he says. ‘Interview Delon. Find out who this man was to him.’

The detectives stand there, open-mouthed.

‘Right,’ Patard says. ‘Let me know what you find.’

Patard glances at the paperwork again. The residency permit lists the dead man as a political refugee. Occupation: doublure – a stand-in. A stand-in, it would seem, for Alain Delon.

Unlike the two detectives, Patard isn’t impressed. He’s never seen a Delon film. Doesn’t plan to. But something tells him – this case is about to get complicated.

Edward Chisholm, author of A Waiter in Paris, was born in England and moved to Paris after graduating from the School of Oriental and African Studies in London. His work has appeared in The New York Times, The Guardian, and The Financial Times magazine. He lives in England.

#7654. Bobcats, “Twin Peaks,” deer: What influenced Gabrielle Lucille Fuentes’ new novel

I love and often teach the memoir People Who Led to My Plays by Adrienne Kennedy. In the book, Kennedy lists all the diverse people, objects, works of art, images, songs, and events that shaped her as an artist. The result is a portrait of a singular artist, a time period, and a manual for becoming an artist.

I have borrowed her form here to explore some of my influences.

Many years ago, my parents sent me a video of a female bobcat being released in the woods outside their home in Northern Wisconsin. It was deep winter, the snow several feet high. An acquaintance of theirs had trapped the bobcat to stop it from terrorizing his neighbor’s chickens and he felt my parents’ woods was a safe place to release her. This news alone would have been interesting enough, but the specifics of the video fascinated me.

The bobcat snarled in the cage, her fluffy winter coat standing on edge, looking both surprisingly small and terrifyingly dangerous. Her captor placed a frozen duck carcass on the snow outside the cage, opened the door, and quickly backed away. But the bobcat didn’t move. She stayed in the cage. The door was open, yet she stayed.

That image captivated me and I started building a story and characters around it.

In my twenties, everyone in my friend group loved Twin Peaks. But I hated it. It frightened me, on many levels, and I hated the way Laura Palmer’s dead and aestheticized body was used to create a story around, a story she had no say in. I wanted to examine this trope of the “beautiful dead girl”: to see if I could write about the real danger women and girls face without making them a spectacle, to see if there was a way to give them agency in a culture that took so much from them.

“—But I love/ life/ I get to be/ in it/ From somewhere else/ in the world/ I am living….”

I consumed all seven episodes ravenously and in quick succession, in the days when I could stay up all night watching TV, letting the images soak into my mind in the thin, vulnerable hours of early morning. I loved the misty forests and the character of the deep, dark lake, the isolation and strangeness. Though the story takes place in New Zealand, the setting felt very similar to places I’d known in Wisconsin. And the missing girl takes action, shapes the story, has a life after the crime that incites the series.

I’d heard and read this folktale, of a mysterious woman completely covered in hair who haunts the jungles of the Caribbean. Her backwards feet confuse those who’d try to track her and her name means “so beautiful” despite or in spite of her sometimes-vengeful nature and her unabashed wildness.

When I saw paintings of her by Firelei Baez—her hair intricately painted fur, her body melding with palms and fauna, her backward feet sprouting kitten heels—the ciguapa began haunting me, stalking in and around my novel.

My family, like countless others, has been irrevocably shaped by the opioid crisis. I carried, and still carry, rage against the Sackler family and others whose criminal and greedy actions caused so much pain and suffering. I wanted to punish them. I wanted to indict them. But I write novels and I didn’t want to write a novel about them. Instead, Clear Water was a way of transforming that rage, of telling the stories of the victims and survivors of this crisis.

In Wisconsin, deer are everywhere. They are full of contradictions: both sustenance and a nuisance—carrying disease, eating flowers and vegetables, totaling cars. They can be both prey and cause destruction. They can seem almost tame, yet are dangerous to approach. They are common and graceful. These contradictions became an intricate part of my book—deer acting as both symbols and forces of their own in the narrative.

Stephen Graham Jones has written many fabulous books since Ledfeather in 2008, but I read this novel at a pivotal moment in the writing of Clear Water. The way Jones interweaves different timelines, the way history shapes the present, and the relationships between humans and animals served as a North Star for my own writing.

I listened to her early albums on repeat while writing Clear Water. Her songs look without faltering at the pain of poverty, violence, and loss yet remain so tender, so full of love and hope.

The forests and lakes of Wisconsin are both the setting of Clear Water and forces that shape the story and the characters. Oaks drop acorns that messages could be carved on. Pines are the only green visible for months in the winter. Birch roots hold the land together. Leaves and pinecones and acorns drop into the lakes, dyeing the water a deep brown tinged with orange.

Even shallow water is opaque. Many beings seek refuge there. Anything could hide there.

Gabrielle Lucille Fuentes is the author of The Sleeping World, Clear Water, and Are We Ever Our Own. She has received fellowships from Hedgebrook, Willapa Bay Artists in Residency, Yaddo, the Millay Colony, Lighthouse Works, and the Blue Mountain Center. She holds a BA from Brown University, an MFA from the University of Colorado, Boulder, and a PhD from the University of Georgia. She is an associate professor at the University of Maryland. She lives in Maryland with her family.

#7653. Satanic Temple can host holiday celebration at state Capitol building, judge rules

The Satanic Temple of Iowa coloring pages. The temple will be allowed to host a family-friendly holiday celebration in the Iowa Capitol building, a federal judge has ruled. (Photo courtesy of Magick Moth Media via the American Civil Liberties Union)

Iowa state officials must allow the Satanic Temple to host a family-friendly holiday celebration in the Iowa Capitol building without conditions or restrictions, a federal judge has ruled.

Chief U.S. District Judge Stephanie Rose of the Southern District of Iowa granted a preliminary injunction Monday ordering the state to approve the Satanic Temple’s application, which has been denied for the past three years despite other religious organizations being approved, Courthouse News Service reports.

The application was denied this year because a state official said the event’s costume contest—featuring a figure from European folklore known as Krampus who carries a stick—would harm children.

Rose reasoned that whether a costume may frighten a child is not a permissible basis for excluding speech, and the entire event cannot be denied simply because someone might carry a stick.

The American Civil Liberties Union and the temple filed the lawsuit in August.

“Congregants of the Satanic Temple have every right to live their authentic religious identity in public and are entitled to the same dignity and the same access to public spaces as members of more familiar traditions,” said temple attorney Matt Kezhaya in a Nov. 2 press release.
